claims.summary: For stress / anxiety, Magnesium is well-supported by human trials (26 studies).

explanation.what_it_is: Magnesium is an essential mineral that acts as a cofactor in over 300 enzymatic reactions throughout the body. It is a key component of chlorophyll in plants and is obtained through diet (nuts, seeds, leafy greens, whole grains) or supplementation.
explanation.how_it_works: Magnesium regulates nerve and muscle function by controlling calcium flow across cell membranes and modulating neurotransmitter release. It activates the parasympathetic nervous system—your body's 'rest and digest' mode—which naturally calms stress responses. In the gut, it draws water into the intestinal lumen, supporting healthy bowel motility. It also helps cells use glucose efficiently and stabilizes blood sugar by supporting insulin signaling and glucose metabolism.

proven_benefits.note: Consistent human evidence (22 studies) shows magnesium supplementation is associated with improved mood and reduced depressive symptoms.
Robust human evidence (35 studies) demonstrates magnesium improves fasting glucose, insulin sensitivity, and metabolic control.
Well-supported human evidence (22 studies) shows magnesium promotes regular bowel function and gut motility.
Strong human evidence (26 studies) indicates magnesium significantly reduces perceived stress and anxiety symptoms.

promising_benefits.note: Early human evidence (10 studies) suggests magnesium may support heart health, but findings are not yet conclusive and require further investigation.

explanation.emerging_research: Recent work explores magnesium's role in migraine prevention, sleep quality optimization, and bone health maintenance, though these areas remain actively studied. The mineral's interaction with the gut microbiome is also an emerging frontier. These applications are promising but not yet established as clinical standards.
explanation.caveats: Magnesium is very safe at dietary doses, but excessive supplementation can cause loose stools or gastrointestinal discomfort. Quality and bioavailability vary by form (citrate, glycinate, and malate are well-absorbed; oxide is poorly absorbed). Individual needs vary widely based on diet and health status; deficiency is common but not universal.
